vignette:
He is 46 and has spent most of his adult life working as a graphic designer, a job that has always suited him because it lets him control details, revise what feels off, and work quietly until a page or image finally looks right. Before the traumatic event, he describes himself as steady, private, and not especially dramatic. He and his wife have been married for many years, and their life together had settled into a familiar rhythm: work, dinners at home, weekend errands, occasional plans with friends that he usually enjoyed once he was there. He did not think of himself as someone who would be deeply affected by a frightening encounter with police. He believed, in his words, that "bad things happen to other people."

That changed on an evening when he is pulled into a police incident that quickly becomes chaotic and humiliating. He recounts that he is mistaken for someone connected to a crime scene and suddenly surrounded by officers who are loud, suspicious, and physically imposing. What begins as confusion turns into fear when he is ordered to the ground, handcuffed, and held there while strangers search him and question him. He keeps returning to the moment of being pressed facedown and unable to explain himself, the sensation of his cheek against cold pavement, the weight of his own panic rising as his chest tightens and his mind blanks. He remembers trying to speak clearly, then hearing his own voice tremble. The officers do not seem to hear him, and that experience of not being believed lodges in him more deeply than the physical force itself.

In the days afterward, he moves through the world feeling as though the event is still unfolding somewhere just behind him. He sleeps lightly and wakes at the smallest sound, already tense before he is fully conscious. At night he replays the scene in fragments: the flash of uniforms, the barking commands, the roughness of the handcuffs, the humiliation of strangers watching. He says the memory does not come back as a complete story but as body sensations - a rush of heat, a surge of nausea, a painful tightness in his jaw and shoulders. Sometimes he finds himself back on the ground in his mind while standing in the kitchen or waiting for coffee. Other times, he notices he has been staring at a wall at work and has lost several minutes without meaning to.

Because he works as a graphic designer, much of his day depends on sustained attention, but that has become difficult. He sits down at his computer and then rechecks the same file repeatedly because he cannot trust himself to finish a task cleanly. He is more irritable when coworkers interrupt him, and he notices that sudden noises in the office - a door slamming, a security alarm, someone stepping up behind his chair - send a jolt through his whole body. He starts avoiding certain situations that remind him of the arrest, especially anything involving police, crowds, or places where he might feel trapped. He changes the route he drives, scans parking lots before getting out of the car, and becomes uneasy when a patrol vehicle passes. Even simple errands can take more effort because he imagines being stopped, questioned, or misread again.

At home, his wife sees how much he has narrowed his world. He is physically present but often distant, and he dislikes talking about what happened because the story makes him feel exposed and foolish. He says he cannot bear the thought that he may always be the person who was taken down in public and unable to stop it. Shame sits close to the fear. He is less affectionate when he is overwhelmed and has trouble relaxing on weekends. He wants to be patient and normal, yet he catches himself scanning exits at restaurants, sitting with his back to the wall, and tensing whenever an unfamiliar man approaches. He becomes upset with himself for being "on edge all the time," but the effort to push it away usually makes it worse.

Over time, he begins to recognize that the trauma has not remained in the past. It enters his body, his work, his marriage, and his ordinary routines. He still completes projects and fulfills obligations, but he does so with more strain, more vigilance, and less ease. He continues to hope that if he stays busy enough, the memory will quiet down, even as the event keeps returning in sleep, in flashbacks of sensation, and in the reflexive fear that he is once again about to be trapped, misunderstood, and powerless.
